slides: Let's continue to the silver triangle. The silver triangle is our own name, there isn't really such a name. We gave it one so the gold triangle won't feel lonely.

slides.say: It's a right triangle that is also isosceles. Here's a picture that helps. Take a square sandwich, and cut it from one corner to the opposite corner. Some students think of a triangle cheese pastry, a borekas.
Each half is exactly this triangle. It has a right angle, the corner of the square, and two equal legs, the two edges of the sandwich. The cut is the hypotenuse.
Let's look at the half on its own, the same triangle. The two legs are equal, so the angles opposite them are equal too. Together they make ninety, so each one is forty-five degrees.
at: Let's look at the half on its own

slides.say: Its sides always keep the ratio a, a, a root two. Let's see why. One leg is a, so the other leg is a too. To find the hypotenuse, we use Pythagoras. a squared plus a squared is two a squared.
Take the root, and the hypotenuse is a times root two. So the sides of the silver triangle are a, a, and a root two. Two legs and the hypotenuse.
at: So the sides of the silver triangle

slides.say: From a leg to the hypotenuse, multiply by root two. From the hypotenuse to a leg, divide by root two. Say a leg is seven. The hypotenuse is seven root two. And of course the other leg is also seven.

Now a hypotenuse of sixteen. The legs are equal, and each is sixteen over root two. Remember the method from the gold triangle, ignore the root. Sixteen divided by two is eight, and put the root two back, eight root two.
And a hypotenuse of six root two? Divide by root two, the roots cancel, and each leg is six.

And a square's diagonal? It's the same triangle. The side of the square is a leg, and the diagonal is the hypotenuse, so the diagonal is the side times root two. Let's solve an example. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
